An Easy Passage – Julia Copus

With a few dazzling images and some audacious sentence structure, “An Easy Passage” vividly paints a tiny snippet of time. The action of the poem lasts for just a few seconds but the reader is left with a series of retina-searing impressions of the girl’s descent towards her waiting friend.

The porch roof is brilliantly characterised as “a square of petrified beach,” which captures the appearance of flat roofing while the adjective doubles up to reflect the fear of the trembling girl. She reaches for the “flimsy, hole-punched, aluminium lever,”...

Colour also plays a key role in making the action of the poem vivid. The girls’ vibrancy: “gold stud / earrings,” “silver anklet” and “shimmering– / oyster-painted toenails” which “flash” emphasises the notion that they are “lit, as if from within” and contrasts with the grey, drab and lifeless world around them.

Crucial to establishing the near-frozen timeframe of the poem is the extensive sentence structure. The whole poem consists of just five sentences, with the final one extending over 20 lines. This sentence creates a sense of immediacy by using the word “now” three times. The moment is cinematic with multiple viewpoints, switching from the narrator describing the descending girl, zooming out to describe the neighbourhood, referencing an absent mother, crossing the road to describe a neighbouring business, morphing into the perspective and voice of a middle-aged onlooker before seamlessly transitioning back to the original narratorial voice of the poem.

Yet there is one further element to the poem which causes the reader to look well beyond the freezeframe action of the passage and to ask some much bigger questions. Shoved in halfway down the poem is this question:

– What can she know
of the way the world admits us less and less
the more we grow?

The poem dramatises a kind of entry into the world as the girl escapes from her own house and descends into the street. The transition is neither easy nor free from danger - despite the claims of the title - and yet is pulled off with bravery and grace. But if this passage into the world is not simple, the above question indicates that things are set to get more difficult.

Before we explore what this question might mean, we should consider who “us” is. The pronoun adds complexity to the poem by changing the status of the narrator. No longer a detached observer, the question casts the narrator as a critical interpreter of the scene and someone with strong opinions about what growing up entails. More than that, it suggests that the narrator is a real person, who has grown up, and presumably suffered through the process.

The two most obvious possible meaning of “us” are 1. Humans and 2. Women. In the first reading, the question would comment on the ways in which humans in general are rejected as they get older. In this sense, it could be a comment on discrimination against older people. Yet there is little in the poem to point to this reading.

On the other hand, there is much to suggest that the concerns of the narrator relate to the treatment of women in general. Support for this reading comes from the fact that the poem is populated solely by females comprising the two girls, the secretary and the absent mother. In addition, the question is inserted directly after (in response to?) a reference to the girl’s “tiny breasts.”

How many times should we read the title of “An Easy Passage”? The pun on “passage” (meaning both text and progression) suggests that we read it twice, but once we have read the poem, we are likely to understand that both of these meanings are skewed with irony. The text may seem simple, but is intricately composed and has a hidden depth, while the progression of the girl into her house may appear easy but is laden with difficult symbolism.

The poem exudes a light simplicity in order to mirror the carefree and unselfconscious nature of the girl. So the free verse
